::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Research into cognitive control has flourished over the last three decades across many areas of the psychological and neural sciences, but problems have recently emerged that raise foundational questions about what cognitive control is, how individual differences should be measured, and the validity of cognitive control as an explanation for variation in behavioral traits and clinical conditions.
Here, we outline a novel perspective that is rooted in evidence accumulation models, formal mathematical models that explain how individuals make choices across many contexts.

We review model-based work that distinguishes conflict-specific processes, which are selectively engaged to address goal-conflicting information, from task-general processes that facilitate goal-relevant responding irrespective of the presence of conflict.
This review reveals an emerging consensus that task-general, but not conflict-specific, processes show validity as coherent individual difference dimensions.
We then highlight the computationally-derived measure we call efficiency of evidence accumulation (EEA) that reflects the amplification of goal-relevant information across many tasks and contexts.

EEA shows strong validity as a trait-like individual difference dimension, explains individual differences in performance in cognitive control tasks, and shows clear relevance to behavioral traits and clinical conditions in which cognitive control, as traditionally defined, is thought to be impaired.

These findings help address multiple theoretical, methodological, and empirical challenges in the study of control processes in cognition, indicate that characterizing processes that enhance goal-relevant responding across contexts is a promising way forward, and suggest important ways in which theories of control's role in behavioral outcomes could be revised.

Cognitive control is a foundational construct in the psychological and neural sciences that is typically characterized as a person's ability to pursue goal-relevant behaviors in the face of habitual or immediately compelling alternatives (Cohen, 2017).

In personality, clinical, and developmental psychology, cognitive control is widely conceptualized as a trait-like individual difference dimension reflecting a person's ability to control their cognition in the service of goals.

In the Stroop task, participants respond based on the color of the word while disregarding irrelevant information about the meaning of the word.

The definition of cognitive control embedded in conflict paradigms, as a process involved in suppressing stimulus information that conflicts with task goals, allows for a high degree of terminological and experimental precision, which likely explains the popularity of these tasks in experimental psychology.

Yet, there is also a tension between this narrow definition and the broader conceptualizations of cognitive control used in other subfields, as a process that amplifies goal-relevant information (e.g., Miller & Cohen, 2001) or as people's trait-like ability to engage in cognitive operations relevant to their goals (e.g., in clinical and developmental psychology).

text.text: Indeed, in other scientific fields, such as control systems engineering (Lamnabhi-Lagarrigue et al., 2017; Murray et al., 2003; Rivera et al., 2007), and in lay discourse, a "control" process is broadly understood to be a process that modulates the operations of other processes in the service of a goal.

text.text: Hence, in this review, we focus on conflict tasks as the predominant paradigm used to experimentally investigate cognitive control, but also conceptualize "control" processes along the lines of this broader, commonly accepted definition as any process that modulates cognitive operations in the service of a goal.
As will become clear, the tension between these narrow and broad conceptualizations of cognitive control has important implications for theory.
Although research into cognitive control has flourished over the last three decades, serious problems have recently come to light that call for a careful reassessment.
The aim of this review is to characterize these problems and argue for a principled way forward.
Section 1 reviews critical problems with conflict tasks, a dominant method used to experimentally investigate cognitive control.
We argue that these problems raise foundational questions about what cognitive control is and how it should be measured.
Against the backdrop of these questions, the following sections chart a way forward.

Conflict tasks are members of a broader class of forced-choice tasks, and evidence accumulation models (EAMs) have emerged as the leading computational models of the mechanisms engaged in forced-choice tasks.

We identify two classes of processes operative in EAMs that are relevant to cognitive control: conflict-specific processes that are engaged by information that actively conflicts with goals, and taskgeneral processes that facilitate goal-congruent responding irrespective of the presence of conflict.
Although theorists have mostly focused on conflict-specific processes, we make a systematic case for the importance of task-general processes to the construct of cognitive control.

More specifically, we review a growing literature on efficiency of evidence accumulation (EEA), a parametric measure derived from EAMs that indexes the efficacy of task-general processes that facilitate the selective gathering of goalrelevant information over goal-irrelevant information when making choices.

We show that, unlike parameters that index conflict-specific forms of control, EEA constitutes a reliable, trait-like individual difference dimension, explains a large portion of the variance in individuals' performance on task-based measures of cognitive control, and shows clear relevance to traits (e.g., self-reported self-control) and psychiatric conditions (e.g., ADHD and substance use) in which control has traditionally been thought to be impaired.
We argue that these findings provide at least two important insights for how cognitive control is understood.
First, studying basic processes that enhance EEA across many contexts could reveal mechanisms of "cognitive control", in the sense that they enhance goal-relevant processes across tasks.

Second, because EEA relates to many individual difference variables that have previously been associated with the construct of cognitive control, EEA is useful explanatory construct for revising theories in fields that have relied on the construct of cognitive control to understand individual differences in behavior.
We conclude with a discussion of theoretical and methodological implications of these emerging insights and consider future directions for research.

text.text: Conflict-Based Measures of Cognitive Control Conflict tasks (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974; Stroop, 1935 Stroop, , 1938) ) (Figure 2A) are the leading method for experimentally investigating cognitive control.

text.text: The "incongruent" condition in conflict tasks involves presentation of irrelevant information that directly contradicts the task goal (e.g., an overlearned verbal cue in the Stroop; peripheral visual information in the Flanker), while in the "congruent" condition the irrelevant information is instead aligned with the goal-relevant response.

In experimental psychology research, cognitive control is assumed to be selectively or preferentially engaged to resolve conflicting stimulus properties in the incongruent condition and to be minimally engaged in the congruent condition.
Another class of "conflict recognition" paradigms, including the frequently used nback task (Figure 2B), seek to illuminate cognitive control in the context of recognition memory.

text.text: The goal in these paradigms is to evaluate whether memory-probe stimuli meet specific "target" criteria (e.g., in the 2-back task: is the current probe the same as that presented two trials back?).
"Novel" probe stimuli that have not been presented recently are easily rejected as non-targets due to their unfamiliarity.

In contrast, "lure" stimuli that were presented recently but do not meet criteria for being a target (e.g., a stimulus presented one trial back in the 2-back task) require individuals to resolve conflict between goal-relevant evidence that the stimulus fails to meet the target criterion and contradictory evidence from stimulus familiarity (Oberauer, 2005).

text.text: Rejection of lures is, therefore, thought to require selective or preferential engagement of cognitive control.

Task-switching paradigms, in which people are cued to switch from one set of stimulus/response mappings to another on a given trial, are also commonly used to study cognitive control (Monsell, 2003; Wylie & Allport, 2000).
text.formatted: Task-switching paradigms, in which people are cued to switch from one set of stimulus/response mappings to another on a given trial, are also commonly used to study cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Monsell, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Wylie & Allport, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Although not typically considered "conflict" tasks, these paradigms similarly assume that cognitive control is selectively or preferentially engaged to resolve conflict between the obsolete task set and the new goal-relevant task set on "switch" trials and to only be minimally engaged on trials that allow the prior task set to be carried forward.

Therefore, despite considerable methodological diversity in task-based measures of cognitive control, these tasks share the fundamental assumption that cognitive control is selectively engaged in situations in which stimulus features or mental processes (e.g., obsolete task sets, task-irrelevant peripheral visual information) that directly contradict task goals are highly influential and must be suppressed or ignored.

Cognitive control is typically indexed in conflict tasks using subtraction methods that contrast behavioral performance metrics in conditions in which cognitive control is thought to be minimally engaged (e.g., congruent trials) versus strongly engaged (e.g., incongruent trials).

If there are, in addition, more general control mechanisms that are involved in selectively enhancing goal-relevant processes across tasks and conditions (which fall under the broader conceptualization of "control" outlined in the introduction) such mechanisms would not be measured by subtracting performance across incongruent and congruent conditions-subtraction would instead remove the signal of interest.
But what could these more general mechanisms be, and how could they be disentangled from other processes?

Computational Models of Choice and Conflict-Specific Versus Task-General Processes Evidence Accumulation Models: A Brief Overview and Recent Developments Conflict tasks are instances of a broader class of tasks that involve speeded forced choices.

In parallel to the growing literature on cognitive control, the last several decades have seen substantial advances in computational modeling frameworks for these tasks that posit formal mathematical explanations for how individuals make decisions, providing quantitative predictions about task performance that have been extensively supported (Busemeyer & Johnson, 2004; Heathcote & Matzke, 2022).

EAMs assume that choices and response times are determined by a process in which people gradually gather noisy evidence from environmental stimuli for each possible choice until an evidence threshold for one choice is first reached.
There are two general EAM architectures.

Diffusion models (Figure 3A) assume that evidence for each choice is collapsed into a relative evidence total that drifts between two boundaries representing each of two response options until a choice is selected when the process terminates at one of the boundaries (Ratcliff et al., 2016).

In sum, two classes of processes within the EAM framework stand out as being potentially relevant to understanding individual differences in performance on cognitive control tasks.

First is a set of "conflict-specific" processes that suppress the early influence of goal-irrelevant evidence and that are reflected in the parameters that describe the early deflection of the decision process in conflict diffusion models and parameters that describe the automatic priming effect in conflict accumulator models.

Second are "task-general" processes that are operative across both the congruent and incongruent conditions in conflict tasks, and likely across many non-conflict tasks as well (a point we elaborate below).
Several EAM parameters offer insights into the potential nature of these task-general processes.

Threshold separation in diffusion models (a) and the average height of the threshold (b) in accumulator models both index an individual's level of caution in responding as higher values of each allow the decision maker to gather a greater amount of evidence before making a choice (Heathcote & Matzke, 2022; Hedge et al., 2019; Ratcliff et al., 2016).

These findings across multiple task paradigms and modeling frameworks converge on a single conclusion: selectively engaged mechanisms that allow individuals to suppress goal-irrelevant evidence in conditions of conflicting information appear to be measurable in multiple conflict tasks and are somewhat stable across time, but the mechanisms measured in these models do not reflect a common construct across tasks.
This raises two possibilities.
The first is that current conflict models are simply inadequate for capturing mechanisms that resolve conflict across diverse tasks.
It is possible that future developments in modeling may provide better evidence for such mechanisms.

The second possibility, which is bolstered by consistent findings that conflict-specific mechanisms show little cross-task validity even under conditions of reliable measurement (Hedge et al., 2022; Molloy et al., 2026; Weigard, Suzuki, et al., 2024), is that these mechanisms reflect real cognitive traits but these traits only have relevance within narrow and idiosyncratic task contexts (e.g., suppressing peripheral visual information in a flanker task or disregarding evidence of stimulus familiarity in an n-back).

Critically, this general EEA factor had a similarly strong influence on behavior across the congruent and incongruent conditions of conflict tasks, as well as across the switch and non-switch trials of two task-switching paradigms.
Therefore, EEA appears to be equally important for driving performance across conditions that both have, and have not, been traditionally assumed to engage cognitive control.
Moreover, in contrast to subtraction metrics, this EEA factor exhibited good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.78-0.81).

Taken together, this growing body of work indicates that task-general EEA is a trait-like individual difference dimension that is critically important for driving performance across cognitive control tasks, as well as across other tasks and conditions not traditionally associated with cognitive control.
A growing array of studies document relationships between EEA and criterion variables that have been linked to cognitive control.

A core challenge faced by computational research programs in cognitive science is that model parameters often have ambiguous mappings to traditional cognitive constructs that originated outside of formal modeling.

text.text: We believe, however, that characterizing the v parameter, or EEA more broadly, as reflecting "processing speed" is likely to create more confusion than clarity.

As introduced in Section 2, although the diffusion model uses a single parameter (v) to capture evidence accumulation dynamics, racing-accumulator models have parameterizations that allow the average quantity of accumulated evidence to be dissociated from the quality of that evidence.
These features of evidence accumulation can vary independently of one another (Figure 5A).

text.text: For example, an individual who can process information very quickly, but who fails to base their decision on goal-relevant information, would make inaccurate responses.

In a racing-accumulator model, this individual would have relatively large quantity of evidence accumulation, reflecting their ability to rapidly accumulate putative (i.e., both correct and misleading) evidence during a trial.
However, the quality of their evidence accumulation would be low, reflecting their failure to base decisions on goal-relevant information.

Of these two distinct features of evidence accumulation, quantity has the most straightforward conceptual link with the traditional notion of "processing speed", as it indexes the speed with which individuals can take up information regardless of the accuracy of that information.
In contrast, evidence quality has little conceptual overlap with, and might vary completely independently of, an individual's "speed of information uptake".

Further, simulations show that evidence quantity has a selective relationship with the most common traditional measure of "processing speed", mean choice RT, while evidence quality instead primarily affects choice accuracy (Weigard et al., 2026).

Taken together, these lines of evidence make a strong case against viewing the task-general EEA factor, as measured by v parameters from the diffusion model and evidence quality parameters from racing-accumulator models, as reflecting the traditional construct of "processing speed".

Rather, this factor reflects how efficiently individuals, across diverse cognitive tasks, can selectively accumulate information relevant to task goals and avoid accumulating information irrelevant to task goals.
What Is EEA's Mechanistic Basis and Ontological Role in Science?

We Posit that Evidence Quality Parameters Reflect, in Part, Mechanisms that Amplify Goal-Relevant Processes Through Top-Down Selection If the conceptualization of the task-general EEA factor as "processing speed" is not warranted, what is the mechanistic basis for this factor?

More specifically, what mechanistic processes could possibly underlie a task-general factor that drives evidence quality parameters by enhancing the selective accumulation of goal-relevant over goal-irrelevant evidence across many different cognitive tasks and domains?

In our conceptualization, an individual's observed rate of goal-relevant evidence accumulation in a given task or condition (v in diffusion models, evidence quality in racing accumulator models) is the product of at least three factors.

The first factor consists of the set of stimulus-specific properties that determine the discriminability of choice options in that task or condition (Stafford & Gurney, 2004; Van Ravenzwaaij et al., 2020), with less discriminable options leading to lower goalrelevant evidence accumulation rates.

text.text: We note that, as EAMs were initially conceived as a method of characterizing experimental effects rather than individual differences, this factor is equivalent to the original interpretation of evidence accumulation parameters (e.g., v as a property of the stimulus).

text.text: As outlined in the previous section, the interpretation of the domain-general component -which we call task-general EEA -as "processing speed" is problematic.

Yet, following directly from the core assumptions of EAMs, it stands to reason that any process that contributes to task-general EEA must influence evidence quality parameters by enhancing the selective accumulation of goalrelevant, as opposed to goal-irrelevant, evidence across tasks.

As has been recently highlighted by Oberauer (2024), plausible mechanisms that could enhance evidence accumulation, amongst others, include the selective activation of a task's specific stimulus-response mappings (i.e., task set), the attentional gating of goal-relevant perceptual information, and the selective retrieval of goal-relevant memory representations.

text.text: Although the respective roles of these possible mechanisms, their relative importance for EEA, and their differential engagement across individual tasks and conditions are not currently clear, a key commonality across them is that they all involve the selective amplification of goal-relevant information.

Thus, we posit that individual differences in task-general EEA reflect, at least in part, the integrity of a set of mechanisms that are involved in the top-down selection of goal-relevant information or of goal-relevant cognitive and neural processes.

We assume that these top-down selection mechanisms are domain-general, in that the processes they support (e.g., task-set activation, perceptual gating, activation of goalrelevant memory representations) would be broadly relevant to improving goal-directed behavior across diverse tasks and contexts, regardless of the specific cognitive domain involved.

Even though the set of possible mechanisms that may be involved in top-down selection is not currently well-characterized, we believe that the goal of better clarifying these mechanisms offers a productive focus for the future scientific investigation of goal-directed behavior and has important implications for how the construct of cognitive control is understood.

text.text: In this section, we clarify that, although we agree that task-general EEA should not be viewed as equivalent to the traditional construct of cognitive control (let alone self-control), findings on EEA have important and specific implications for scientific fields that have relied on this construct.

As a starting point, consider that the task-general ability indexed by EEA bears a striking connection with the foundational conceptualization of cognitive control referenced at the beginning of this article: the ability to use top-down bias signals to selectively amplify the processing of information relevant to an individual's current goals (Miller, 2000; Miller & Cohen, 2001) (Figure 1).

text.text: If such a top-down process, or a set of multiple top-down processes, was successful at amplifying goal-relevant information, this amplification would necessarily be directly reflected in EEA estimates given that EEA is an explicit measure of the degree to which individuals selectively accumulate goal-relevant information.

In experimental, developmental, and clinical research, cognitive control has been conceptualized as a trait-like cognitive individual difference dimension that explains individual differences in performance in conflict tasks and that contributes to an array of broader behavioral traits (e.g., self-control) and clinical conditions (e.g., ADHD, substance use).

The evidence reviewed earlier shows that the abilities indexed by EEA do in fact form a trait-like individual difference dimension, that this dimension explains individual differences across diverse laboratory tasks, including those traditionally assumed to measure cognitive control, and that EEA shows clear connections with control-relevant behavioral traits and clinical conditions.
Thus, EEA appears to fill several of the theoretical and functional roles closely associated with the legacy construct of cognitive control.
Further, there are several additional connections between EEA and common conceptualizations of cognitive control.
Traditionally, cognitive control has been hypothesized to suppress or inhibit inappropriate automatic or habitual responses, thus leading to the widespread use of conflict tasks to study control.
Interestingly, the processes indexed by EEA do, in fact, play a functional role in reducing the influence of automatic processes that conflict with task goals.
This is most clearly brought out in conflict EAMs, in which two kinds of independent processes compete for influence on incongruent trials (Figure 4).

text.text: Processes underpinning automaticity exert early influences that favor the incorrect response, while processes underpinning EEA exert later-onset, sustained influences that favor the correct response.
These influences combine additively, and since on incongruent trials they have opposite signs, EEA does in fact oppose automatic processes and reduces their influence on the eventual choice.
Importantly, we do not claim that processes indexed by EEA play any specific role in inhibiting evidence driven by conflicting features.
As we have emphasized throughout, the processes indexed by EEA are task-general, and they amplify goal-relevant information irrespective of the presence of conflicting automatic influences.

Hence, our claim is entirely consistent with the assumption of current conflict EAMs that behavior on conflict tasks is determined by two distinct categories of processes (conflict-specific and task-general) that are conceptually independent of one another but have opposing influences on choices made on incongruent trials.
Another notable connection between EEA and cognitive control pertains to the neural correlates of EEA.

Decades of theoretical and empirical research have localized cognitive control functions to brain regions in the prefrontal cortex and the broader frontoparietal network (Friedman & Robbins, 2022; Menon & D'Esposito, 2022b; Miller, 2000; Miller & Cohen, 2001).

text.text: This relationship was replicated across two diverse samples of youth and young adults.

The association was also similarly strong regardless of whether EEA was obtained from a task typically assumed to measure cognitive control (2-back) or a task that has not traditionally been assumed to measure cognitive control (a "0-back", or simple recognition memory, task), underscoring the task-general nature of EEA and its neural correlates.

Therefore, task-general EEA not only plays similar functional roles to the construct of cognitive control in explaining individual differences in behavior but also shows important associations with neural features that have long been associated with the construct.

To summarize, the task-general EEA factor has important links with foundational conceptualizations of cognitive control; hypothesized control processes that amplify goal-relevant information would be expected to be reflected in evidence quality parameters and task-general EEA, which largely drives individual variation in evidence quality parameters, relates to behavioral individual differences and brain features that have previously been linked to cognitive control.
Despite these connections, we caution that viewing EEA as a measure of, or substitute for, the construct of cognitive control, is not appropriate for several reasons.

First, although EEA displays several conceptual links with the construct of cognitive control, its task-general nature is in direct opposition to popular conceptualizations of cognitive control as being selectively engaged in conditions of explicit conflict between relevant and irrelevant information, a disconnect we address in the next subsection.

Second, although mechanisms involved in top-down selection of goal-relevant information or other "control" mechanisms that amplify goal-relevant processes would be expected to be reflected in EEA, alternative processes that have little to do with selection or control may also impact task-general EEA.
Indeed, as EEA is almost certainly multidetermined (Weigard & Sripada, 2021), it is not at all safe to assume that EEA reflects any one specific process alone.

text.text: Finally, the problems described above with the tendency to equate EEA with the legacy construct of "processing speed" show the perils of trying to map formal cognitive model parameters on to older psychological constructs that were derived from verbal theories (Weigard et al., 2026).

text.text: Hence, attempting to equate, or replace, the traditional construct of cognitive control with the EEA factor is inappropriate and would likely lead to more confusion than clarity.
Nonetheless, we argue that the growing literature on task-general EEA has at least two broad implications for the study of cognitive control.

First, the fact that a large portion of the variance in evidence quality parameters across diverse tasks appears to be explained by task-general EEA suggests there are likely mechanistic processes that are involved in selectively amplifying goal-relevant information across many tasks and cognitive domains.
The study of such processes has the potential to reveal novel mechanisms of "control", in that such processes modulate the operations of other cognitive processes in service of individuals' goals.

The second implication is that, because EEA relates to many behavioral outcomes and neuroimaging variables that have previously been associated with the construct of cognitive control, EEA is useful explanatory construct for revising theories in fields that have relied on the construct of cognitive control to understand individual differences in behavior (e.g., clinical and personality psychology, psychiatric neuroscience).

We outline below, at the end of Section 6, our proposal that EEA can operate as a valuable "fulcrum construct" linking the study of basic mechanisms that enhance goal-relevant processes across cognitive tasks to the study of individual differences in goal-directed behavior.

But first, we address the important caveat that our view of task-general EEA shows a fundamental disconnect with the common assumption that, for a process to be considered a "cognitive control" process, it must be selectively engaged in conditions of conflict.

We have contrasted the task-general processes indexed by EEA with the conflictselective processes that are also identifiable in EAMs and argued that the former are likely to be relevant to the construct of cognitive control while the latter are unlikely to represent a coherent cross-task factor or to be related to individual differences in goaldirected behavior.
Yet this assertion displays a key contradiction with the way that cognitive control has been conceived by many theorists in the field.
Cognitive control, has often (though not universally) been thought to be selectively or preferentially engaged by conflict (Oberauer, 2024).

text.text: Thus, the processes indexed by EEA deviate in a key way from this widely adopted conception of cognitive control.

As discussed in the Introduction, the view that cognitive control must be selectively engaged in conditions of conflict is a core assumption of research on conflict tasks and is particularly influential in experimental psychology due to the terminological and experimental precision that this assumption affords.

However, this narrow experimental definition of cognitive control is not widely shared across other areas in the behavioral and brain sciences, which describe control as a more general process that amplifies goal-relevant information (e.g., Miller & Cohen, 2001) or as individual differences in people's ability to engage in cognitive operations that are relevant to their goals (e.g., in personality or clinical psychology).

text.text: How might the field resolve these terminological ambiguities?

Constructs posited by scientists frequently undergo revision and refinement over time as a better understanding of the target system emerges, and it is typical to allow some flexibility to the meanings of scientific terms as mechanistic knowledge grows, as has been discussed extensively in the philosophy of science (Kitcher, 1993).

text.text: For example, Aristotle thought "stars" are holes in the firmament that encases the universe, allowing rays of light to enter.
As scientific knowledge grew, astronomy did not reject the idea that there are stars, but it instead recognized that early Aristotelian claims about them turned out to be false.

Similarly, if the task-general EEA factor reflects, in part, processes that selectively modulate other cognitive operations in a top-down manner to amplify goalrelevant information, we think it would be appropriate infer that "cognitive control" processes exist, but that the common assumption that such processes must be selectively engaged is false.

The alternative is to conclude that, because experimental conflict task research has failed to identify selectively engaged cognitive control processes, "cognitive control" does not exist and should therefore be forever banished from the scientific lexicon.

Although such a conclusion may maintain terminological precision within subfields of experimental psychology, we believe that any benefit would be overshadowed by the problematic effect it would have on broader scientific discourse by implying that "control" processes, defined as those that modulate other processes in top-down manner in the interest of goals, do not exist.
In the end, however, we believe that this disagreement is somewhat semantic.

The deeper underlying substantive point is that the task-general processes indexed by EEA play important theoretical and empirical roles: they amplify goal-relevant information, they form a trait-like individual difference dimension, they are related to traits and conditions of significant practical and clinical importance, they are underpinned by distinctive neural circuitry, and so on.
These underlying points are unaffected by whether we consider the task-general processes indexed by EEA to be forms of "cognitive control" or not.

Putting these semantic considerations aside, we argue in the following section that the study of EEA has great potential for establishing novel connections between research programs focused on the mechanistic processes underlying goal-directed cognition and broader research programs on individual differences in self-control and associated clinical conditions.
EEA Represents a Valuable "Fulcrum Construct" Linking Lower-Level Neurocognitive Mechanisms with Higher-Level Goal-Directed Behaviors
In order for the study of EEA to be beneficial to scientific research programs, the ontological status of EEA requires some clarification.

One important question concerns whether EEA should be viewed as reflecting a mechanism that explains goal-directed behavior or a parameter (or a computational variable) that simply describes patterns in data but does not in itself have mechanistic meaning.
A related question is whether EEA is a unitary "thing" or is a composite of many things.
Our answers to both questions are nuanced: it depends on the level of analysis at which a given theorist or research program is working.

To illustrate how a scientific construct can simultaneously operate as a descriptive parameter and an explanatory mechanism at different levels of analysis, we first consider an illustrative example from a different area of science: cold fronts, a construct studied in atmospheric physics and meteorological forecasting.
Empirically, a cold front is defined as the leading edge of a mass of cool and dense air that advances to replace a warmer air mass.

Cold fronts are formed by the combination of multiple interacting causal factors, including wind patterns in the upper atmosphere, differences in solar heating of air at different latitudes, low pressure systems that sweep cooler air southward, and the tendency of cold dense air to slide underneath warm air.

In this way, an atmospheric physicist studying the lower-order physical mechanisms that govern shifts in air masses would view the cold front as a descriptive construct; it is a description of a higher-level phenomenon that reflects the aggregate effect of interactions between lower-level physical mechanisms and it is impossible to attribute a given cold front to any one of these specific mechanisms alone.

However, for a scientist focused on meteorological forecasting, a research area that operates at a higher level of analysis than basic atmospheric physics, the cold front has proven to be an extremely valuable explanatory construct.
Cold fronts can be easily identified and modeled and they provide clear, causal explanations for why weather patterns (e.g., rain, thunderstorms) occur at specific places and times.

We posit that EEA similarly operates as a descriptive construct for researchers working at the lower level of understanding basic neurocognitive processes that support the accumulation of goal-relevant information but as an explanatory construct for researchers who seek to provide causal explanations for individual differences in clinical and behavioral outcomes.

text.text: Here, we believe that it is indeed appropriate to view EEA, or at least the high-level, multidetermined process that it indexes, as both a unitary mechanism and as an explanatory construct that can, in the same way that cold fronts provide causal explanations for weather patterns, explain these behavioral outcomes.

Since EEA is a well-characterized summary measure of how well an individual is able to base their choices on information that is relevant to their current goals, it provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for why a given individual may be more or less consistent in their ability to make choices that serve their goals in real-world situations.

In this way, we argue that EEA serves as a valuable fulcrum construct that can be used to bridge the gap between basic research programs focused on the lower-level mechanisms of cognitive task performance and higher-level research programs focused on understanding differences in behavioral outcomes across development, across individuals, and across clinical disorders.

EAMs' clear mathematical specification and well-characterized relations with neurophysiological processes (Gold & Shadlen, 2007; Heathcote & Matzke, 2022; Ratcliff et al., 2016; Shadlen & Kiani, 2013; Smith & Ratcliff, 2004) can likely be leveraged to provide greater mechanistic clarity about the top-down selection processes that support individuals' EEA.

text.text: In turn, EEA's parsimonious definition and excellent psychometric properties would allow these lower-level mechanistic processes to be linked to substantive differences in real-world human behavior and clinical conditions.

Hence, although the precise mechanisms that support task-general EEA have yet to be clarified, EEA nonetheless provides the field with a promising framework for linking basic neurocognitive mechanisms to real-world manifestations of goal-directed behaviors.
>Key Implications and Future Directions
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Key Implications and Future Directions</head>

text.text: In the preceding sections, we have presented evidence from a growing body of EAM research that addresses several of the key theoretical and empirical puzzles in the study of cognitive control.

This work distinguishes two distinct categories of processes that are potentially relevant to the construct of cognitive control: 1) conflict-specific processes, which suppress information that directly conflicts with task goals, and 2) task-general processes that facilitate the selective accumulation of goal-relevant evidence irrespective of the presence of conflict and that would be expected to be reflected in the task-general EEA factor.

We have detailed evidence that conflict-specific processes appear to be idiosyncratic to specific conflict tasks, do not form a cohesive individual difference dimension, and appear to be at best weakly related to behavioral traits and clinical conditions in which control is thought to be impaired.

These lines of evidence all converge on the conclusion that the field's conceptualization of cognitive control as a unitary trait that is selectively or preferentially engaged in conditions of explicit conflict is not supported by evidence and is unlikely to be a useful direction for understanding goal-directed behavior unless these critical problems are resolved.
In contrast, we highlight the burgeoning literature on the task-general EEA factor as being relevant to construct of cognitive control.

We assembled evidence that EEA is a unitary trait-like construct that drives evidence quality parameters across diverse cognitive tasks irrespective of their conflict resolution demands and that it shows robust relations with behavioral traits and clinical conditions in which control is thought to be impaired.

We provide evidence that EEA should not be understood as "processing speed" and instead represents an individual's general ability to accumulate goalrelevant, as opposed to goal-irrelevant, information across tasks.

As cognitive control processes have traditionally been conceptualized as processes that selectively amplify goal-relevant information, it follows that, if such processes exist, they will impact evidence quality parameters.
If processes that selectively amplify goal-relevant information were to operate across diverse tasks, their integrity should, therefore, be reflected in the general EEA factor.

Hence, we posit that an individual's EEA likely reflects, at least in part, the integrity of underlying mechanistic processes that selectively amplify goal-relevant information and that may be thought of as forms of cognitive control if they are better characterized in future work.

Finally, we proposed that EEA represents a useful fulcrum construct for linking basic research programs focused on the mechanistic neurocognitive processes that facilitate goal-directed cognition to higher-level research programs focused on individual differences in self-control and the etiology of clinical conditions in which control is thought to be impaired (e.g., ADHD and substance use).
Beyond highlighting the promise of EEA as a valuable fulcrum construct for the field, our argument has several other key implications for the study of cognitive control.
We now detail these implications and identify critical directions for future work in this area, below.
The Need for Top-Down Selection Is Ubiquitous, Urging a Rethink of How to Study Processes Relevant to Successful Goal Pursuit

The dominant view in cognitive science has been that processes involved in goal-directed behavior must be selectively or preferentially engaged in situations in which stimuli or mental processes that directly conflict with one's goals are active and must therefore be overcome (e.g., incongruent conditions of conflict tasks).
As detailed above, this "incongruent selectivity" assumption is reflected in the subtraction methodology widely used to analyze conflict tasks.

However, if EEA represents one of the key cognitive individual difference dimensions that supports goal-directed behavior, as is suggested by a growing body of clinical and individual differences research, it is notable that EEA does not appear to be preferentially or selectively engaged by conflict.

Instead, when EEA factors are formed from task batteries consisting of diverse conflict tasks, similar loadings for EEA are observed for incongruent conditions that involve stimulus conflict and congruent conditions in which stimulus conflict is absent (Weigard, Clark, et al., 2021).

text.text: The preceding observations suggest that if we understand EEA as reflecting the integrity of mechanisms involved in the top-down selection of goal-relevant information, then these mechanisms operate ubiquitously: they appear to be important for performance on any task in which the subject has a specific task goal and must accumulate evidence from stimuli that is relevant to achieving that goal, a category that arguably subsumes almost all experimental choice tasks used in cognitive science, however simple.
The generality of processes indexed by EEA raises the need for a key distinction between conflict and task relevance.
In conflict, for example the incongruent condition of the Stroop task, there is goal-irrelevant information that opposes the selection of the goal-congruent response.
Neutral or goal-irrelevant information, in contrast, merely weakens the impact of goal-relevant information on response selection.

If EEA reflects the functioning of mechanisms that promote task relevance, boosting activation of goalrelevant information over goal-irrelevant information, this could explain why such mechanisms are ubiquitously engaged.

For example, the need to focus on task relevant information is present even in the simplest perceptual discrimination tasks that have no explicit experimental manipulations of conflicting information.

To successfully complete such tasks, individuals must preferentially gather evidence from the goalrelevant stimulus dimension as opposed to the many other irrelevant stimulus dimensions that are available, preferentially activate the appropriate stimulus/response mappings from many other possible mappings, and preferentially activate memory representations relevant to the goals of the current task as opposed to representations relevant to other potentially salient goals (e.g., making dinner after finishing the study).

This point can be sharpened by recognizing that information that is goalirrelevant but does not explicitly bias choice towards the incorrect response can still negatively impact choice behavior and must be discounted relative to goal-relevant information.

text.text: Importantly, a key implication of (approximate) likelihood ratio-based evidence accumulation is that including "neutral" evidence that equally favors all options reduces the accuracy of decisions.
For example, compare a simple case where 4 units of evidence favor one option and 2 units favor the other, so that the first option is favored by a 2:1 ratio.
If we add 2 units of neutral evidence equally to each option, their ratio becomes 1.5, and so the first option is now less strongly favored.
This illustrates why goal-irrelevant information, even if it is neutral with respect to the response it favors, degrades choice performance.
Hence, prioritizing goal-relevant over goal-irrelevant information, even if the irrelevant information is "neutral", is critical for goal-congruent responding.

Importantly, this ability enhances goal-congruent responding across a wide range of tasks, and not just in incongruent conditions of conflict tasks in which the goalirrelevant information actively opposes the goal-congruent response.
In sum, it has been widely assumed that processes relevant to goal-directed behavior are selectively or preferentially engaged in the incongruent condition of conflict tasks.

We have, however, distinguished the notion of conflict between stimuli from a separate notion of the task relevance of stimuli, and argued that EEA reflects, at least in part, processes that promote task relevance by prioritizing goal-relevant information over goal-irrelevant information.

Since task relevance is a factor in all choice tasks used in cognitive science, from complex conflict tasks to simple perceptual discrimination tasks, this helps explain why the processes indexed by EEA show a ubiquitous influence on behavior.

Acknowledgement of the ubiquitous importance of task relevance and the functional role of processes that promote task relevance for furthering goal-directed behavior has broad implications for developmental, clinical, and individual differences research programs that are currently strongly influenced by selective influence assumptions.

Despite the widespread tendency to ascribe individuals' goal-directed behavior to processes that selectively influence behavior in conditions of conflict, there is now solid evidence that these processes do not form a cohesive individual difference dimension and that they are not linked to behavioral traits and clinical conditions in which goal-directed behavior is thought impaired.
Therefore, a continued focus on conflict-specific processes in these individual differences fields appears untenable.

On the other hand, if processes reflected in the general EEA factor that broadly enhance the processing of task-relevant information do represent important individual difference dimensions relevant to cognitive performance, behavioral outcomes, and clinical conditions, the selective influence assumption should be explicitly avoided for measuring these processes.

Since the general EEA factor drives performance similarly across both the incongruent and congruent conditions of conflict tasks, the selectivity assumption violated and subtraction methods would lead variance relevant to goaldirected behavior to be removed.

Overall, we argue that, for the study of goal-directed behavior, a focus on cognitive and neural mechanisms that amplify the accumulation of goal-relevant information across many tasks and contexts is likely to provide more insights than on a continued focus on processes that are thought to be selectively engaged in a narrow set of cognitive tasks or experimental conditions.
As outlined above, EEA's relations with psychopathology have been gradually coming into focus.

EEA shows clear negative relations with externalizing disorders such as ADHD and substance use, fairly consistent negative relations with thought disorders and major depressive disorder diagnoses, but weaker evidence of relations with depression symptoms at the population level and even some evidence for positive associations with internalizing and anxiety symptoms.
Given these associations, how should EEA be conceptualized within dimensional models of psychopathology and adaptive functioning?

We argue that EEA is a cognitive dimension that represents an important common denominator of risk for disorders that are characterized problems with selfcontrol, goal-directed cognition, and decision-making, which include the externalizing and thought disorder diagnoses with which EEA is convincingly linked.
As a transdiagnostic mechanism, EEA alone clearly cannot possibly explain what makes each of these separate clinical conditions unique.

However, this is highly consistent with the multi-determined nature of most clinical disorders that is now generally acknowledged, such as in the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework (Cuthbert & Insel, 2013; Michelini et al., 2021; Morris et al., 2022) and other modern dimensional psychopathology models.

text.text: EEA is likely just one cognitive factor that interacts with many other trait dimensions of functioning (e.g., RDoC dimensions including positive and negative valence systems, reward processes, social processes, etc.) and environmental circumstances to lead to the emergence of diverse clinical phenotypes.

This doesn't necessarily take away from EEA's importance as a risk factor, but it instead indicates that the field needs to better understand how EEA's interactions with other dimensions of functioning convey risk for specific clinical conditions.

Furthermore, given that EEA itself is likely multidetermined, as we have highlighted above, better understanding the lower-level processes that enhance processing of goal-relevant information across diverse tasks may highlight different causes of EEA impairments in different disorders.

Another important implication of the general EEA factor is that many of the different cognitive measures that are currently used in psychopathology research, such as those aimed at dissociating specific "executive functions" (Friedman & Robbins, 2022), may predominantly reflect EEA rather than the wider array of specific dimensions that they were originally designed to measure.

text.text: As has been previously pointed out (Weigard & Sripada, 2021), the "fractionation" paradigm in clinical neuroscience that aimed to distinguish psychiatric disorders on the basis of cognitive task performance alone has largely failed; cognitive impairments in disorders are typically found across many domains rather than being selectively linked to the specific domains that are hypothesized to be impaired (e.g., disinhibition in ADHD).

text.text: The general EEA factor can explain these findings of broad impairments, and suggests that, although lab-based cognitive tasks clearly contain information that is relevant to self-control and psychopathology, the relevant processes appear to be largely task-general rather than localized to the specific functions that have been the focus of the field (e.g., conflict suppression, working memory, cognitive flexibility).
This raises what might appear to be an important paradox to researchers studying the cognitive basis of psychopathology.
As mentioned above, the single dimension of EEA clearly cannot, on its own, explain the emergence of each of the unique clinical conditions that it is linked to (e.g., psychosis versus ADHD).
Yet, thus far, many of the tasks the field has designed to measure dissociable dimensions of functioning, at least in the cognitive domain, seem to predominantly reflect EEA.

We argue that this paradox can be explained by the fact that many of the other relevant dimensions that may interact with EEA to lead to diverse clinical outcomes are simply outside of the cognitive domain (e.g., positive and negative valence systems, reward processes) or are difficult to measure in the context of controlled lab-based cognitive tasks.

Put another way, even if individual differences in laboratory task-based measures that are currently classified as part of the cognitive domain of RDoC can largely be attributed to the single dimension of EEA, we should not forget about the wide array of dimensions from the five other domains of RDoC, or as-of-yet undiscovered domains, that could interact with cognition to explain clinical outcomes.
It is also certainly possible that cognitive paradigms can be improved to better dissociate more specific dimensions of cognitive functioning that are relevant to psychopathology.

Lasagna et al., 2025) and analyses of cognitive task data in large samples (Blain et al., 2025) has converged to suggest that performance on social cognition tasks reflects a dimension that is dissociable from taskgeneral EEA and has separate clinical correlates.

text.text: Although these areas show great promise for dissociating specific cognitive functions beyond EEA, clinical and individual differences researchers seeking to index EEA as a general cognitive dimension relevant to self-control and psychopathology may be able to simplify their current approaches to measuring cognition.
Data collection for studies in this area often features long batteries of tasks that are hypothesized to selectively engage cognitive control or different "executive" functions.

However, as EEA appears to be a strong task-general dimension that is measurable via even relatively simple choice tasks, the careful curation of tasks traditionally thought to be involved in different cognitive control processes is likely unnecessary.
Instead, researchers can likely obtain a valid measure of the task-general EEA factor through the inclusion of 3-4 relatively simple and efficient choice tasks from different domains.
In archival data sets, a very broad range of forced choice tasks, from simple perceptual tasks to complex conflict tasks, can also be used to measure EEA.

Put another way, if most current laboratory tasks designed to measure cognitive functions relevant to goal-directed behavior primarily relate to relevant behavioral outcomes through the single dimension of EEA, we may as well rely on a smaller set of simple and efficient tasks.

The Need to Dissociate Top-Down Selection Processes That Impact EEA and Potentially Other EAM Parameters As we note above, although we believe it is reasonable to assume that EEA likely reflects multiple underlying mechanisms involved in the top-down selection of goalrelevant perceptual information, task sets, or memory representations, more needs to be known about these potential mechanisms and how they should be characterized and measured.

The apparent ubiquity of task-general EEA across many paradigms and experimental conditions significantly adds to this challenge, because using experiments to dissociate processes is a central tool for understanding such basic mechanisms.

In this way, we think further refinement of EAMs and other formal mathematical models would be helpful for positing potential top-down selection mechanisms and making specific predictions about their manifestations in empirical data, including in new experimental manipulations.

The merging of EAMs with latent variable models shows particular promise in this regard (Stevenson et al., 2024, in press), as this joint modeling framework can simultaneously model mechanistic processes the underlie task performance and determine whether such processes represent robust individual differences constructs.

Another important area of inquiry concerns the potential influence of top-down selection processes or "control" processes (as broadly defined outside of the field of experimental conflict task research) that may impact other EAM parameters.

As noted in Section 4, parameters representing response caution and non-decision times show a similar task-general influence to EEA, but the literature currently indicates that these parameters have more ambiguous relations with relevant criterion measures.

text.text: A similar "componential" approach connects EEA with general cognitive ability (i.e., general intelligence), especially fluid intelligence which relates to online problemsolving abilities.

Tests of fluid intelligence, such as Raven's progressive matrices, require the test taker to perform numerous basic decision operations regarding how to approach the problem, how to execute a search for solutions, when to deviate from the current strategy or backtrack, and so forth.
Individuals with lower EEA are less likely to execute these steps in goal-congruent ways, resulting in poorer performance on the overall task.

text.text: Testing elements of these componential explanations for EEA's relations with self-control and intelligence is a critical focus of future research.
Furthermore, these connections raise a more general question of whether task-general EEA is functionally equivalent to the construct of general intelligence.

In addition to noting the previously discussed perils of equating parameters from formal modeling with traditional psychometric constructs, we highlight important distinctions between EEA and intelligence.

Whereas intelligence is primarily a descriptive construct based on the observation that performance on many different tasks is correlated, EEA is drawn from a formal process model that has specific assumptions that can be quantitatively related to mechanisms determining choice behavior, several of which have been linked to specific neurobiological processes.
Overall, then, EEA is a more specific, parsimoniously defined, statistically estimable, and biologically translatable construct than intelligence.
It thus has greater promise for providing mechanistic clarity about processes that support cognitive performance across tasks (e.g., top-down selection).

This review has detailed pressing problems with the current literature on the construct of cognitive control and has presented a novel perspective on these problems that is rooted in the burgeoning literature on computational models of choice.

It suggests that there are two distinct categories of processes that may be relevant to implementing control during experimental tasks: conflict-specific processes that are engaged to oppose goal-inconsistent information and task-general processes that facilitate the processing of goal-relevant information irrespective of the presence of conflict.

Although conflict-specific processes have garnered the bulk of attention, we highlight the importance of task-general processes that impact evidence quality parameters in EAMs and that are reflected in the general EEA factor.

In contrast to conflict-specific processes, the task-general EEA factor represents a cohesive individual difference dimension, explains individual differences in performance across diverse cognitive tasks, including those thought to reflect control, and is linked to relevant behavioral traits and clinical conditions.
These findings impact the field of cognitive control in two major ways.

First, they highlight the benefits of understanding mechanistic processes involved in the selective amplification of goal-relevant information across tasks as an important direction for understanding goal-directed behavior.

Second, they suggest that EEA is a useful explanatory construct for revising theories in fields that have relied on the traditional construct of cognitive control to understand individual differences in self-control and related clinical conditions and behavioral outcomes.

Moving forward, computational models of choice are likely to provide a valuable general framework for research on cognitive control (defined broadly as cognitive processes that modulate other processes in the service of goals) and related constructs (such as selfcontrol and general intelligence), allowing theorists to take advantage of the large and growing body of theory and empirical findings surrounding these mathematically specified and biologically plausible approaches to understanding mechanisms of adaptive behavior.
